advances:
A compatible common core gives an explicit continuous log-concave output at one integral fiber, with every source marginal physically dominated by its original measure. The construction repairs the supplied box example that obstructs compulsory uniform source marginals and bounded entropy: for every dimension it retains at least \((3/7)2^{-n}W\), although its actual entropy relative to the original target uniform law grows with the dimension. It uses a free log-concave reference and partial original stocks, without renewing any output.

No general retained-mass floor for arbitrary convex bodies is asserted. The missing intermediate claim for this particular mechanism is the existence of a compatible common core and reflected source set with sufficiently large core volume times number of pairs. The construction and its original-capacity consumer are valid; that geometric existence claim remains unproved. Failure of such a claim would obstruct this common-core mechanism, not all partial-stock transports.

One tractable separating test is the following planar inequality. For a rational convex polygon \(C\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\), use all its positive lattice-fiber lengths \(w_I\) and put
\[
\mathcal B(C)=
\max_{\substack{J\in\mathbb Z,\ k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\\
                  J-k,J+k\in D}}
(k+1)\min\{w_{J-k},w_{J+k}\}.
\]
Prove or disprove \(\mathcal B(C)\ge W/4\) for every such polygon with \(W>0\). This is a finite inequality in the actual fiber table. Convexity and an explicit affine shear turn each term into a compatible common core, as verified below; a positive answer therefore produces output mass at least \(W/8\) in this test class. This test concerns the construction, without imposing the centroid or uniform law of an original fiber.

proof:
Choose \(\mathbf q\in\operatorname{int}K\). The following cutoff ensures continuity of the density even at its support boundary. Let
\[
p_K(\mathbf v)=\inf\{t\ge0:\mathbf v\in t(K-\mathbf q)\},
\qquad
g(\mathbf x)=\min\{1,\,2d(1-p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q))_+\}.
\tag{6}
\]
The gauge \(p_K\) is finite, convex, and continuous. Indeed, \(K-\mathbf q\) contains an origin-centered ball of some radius \(r>0\); convexity gives subadditivity and positive homogeneity of the gauge, and these give
\(p_K(\mathbf v)-p_K(\mathbf w)\le p_K(\mathbf v-\mathbf w)\le\|\mathbf v-\mathbf w\|/r\), together with the reverse inequality obtained by interchanging \(\mathbf v,\mathbf w\). Also \(K-\mathbf q=\{\mathbf v:p_K(\mathbf v)\le1\}\), by compactness and the definition of the gauge.

Thus \(g\) is continuous on all of \(\mathbb R^d\), is zero outside \(K\) and on its boundary, and satisfies \(0\le g\le\mathbf1_K\). It is positive in the interior. On \(K\) it is the minimum of the constant function one and the nonnegative concave function \(2d(1-p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q))\). The minimum is concave because its hypograph is the intersection of two convex hypographs. Nonnegative concavity on a convex support implies log-concavity: the concavity inequality followed by weighted arithmetic-geometric mean proves the log-concavity inequality when both endpoint values are positive, while a zero endpoint value makes its right side zero. The extension by zero therefore is log-concave on the whole space.

Put \(G=\int g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\). On the homothetic body \(\mathbf q+(1-1/(2d))(K-\mathbf q)\) the density is one. Bernoulli's inequality gives
\[
0<G\le\mathcal L^d(K),
\qquad
G\ge\left(1-\frac1{2d}\right)^d\mathcal L^d(K)
\ge\frac12\mathcal L^d(K).
\tag{7}
\]

Partition \(E\) into its reflection orbits. For a two-element orbit \(\{\mathbf I,\mathbf I'\}\), where \(\mathbf I'=2\mathbf J-\mathbf I\), push the finite measure \(g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\) forward under the two-source map
\[
\mathbf x\longmapsto
\bigl(\mathbf b+A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)+\mathbf x,
      \mathbf b+A(\mathbf I'-\mathbf J)+\mathbf x\bigr).
\tag{8}
\]
Give these two sources barycentric coefficients \(1/2,1/2\). This is a source coupling of mass \(G\), not a prescribed uniform source coupling. Its continuous output is \(\mathbf b+\mathbf x\), and its base output is exactly \(\mathbf J\). If \(\mathbf J\in E\), its singleton orbit supplies the one-source coupling which is the pushforward of \(g(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\) by \(\mathbf x\mapsto\mathbf b+\mathbf x\), with barycentric coefficient one. It has the same mass and output law.

The actual marginal at a source \(\mathbf I\in E\) is
\[
d\nu_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf y)
=g\bigl(\mathbf y-\mathbf b-A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)\bigr)
  \,d\mathbf y
\le\mathbf1_{C_{\mathbf I}}(\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y
=d\mu_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf y).
\tag{9}
\]
The inequality follows pointwise from (1) and \(g\le\mathbf1_K\); translations have Jacobian one. Reflection orbits partition \(E\), so no index is charged by two different couplings. Thus (9) checks aggregate physical marginal domination, not merely a scalar budget. The couplings directly use these submeasures of the original \(\mu_{\mathbf I}\). No output measure is used as an input to another coupling.

Convexity of \(C\) shows \(\mathbf b+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\): for a pair, the midpoint of the two source points in (8), at any \(\mathbf x\in K\), is \((\mathbf J,\mathbf b+\mathbf x)\); for the singleton this inclusion is already (1). Since \(E\) is nonempty, one of these arguments applies. Summing the \(k_E\) output laws gives exactly
\[
d\kappa_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf y)
=k_E g(\mathbf y-\mathbf b)\,d\mathbf y,
\qquad M=k_EG.
\tag{10}
\]
This density is nonzero, continuous, and log-concave, and (7) proves (2).

For any closed ambient halfspace, an output in the halfspace has at least one source point in it. Indeed, if all source scores were strictly below the defining threshold, their barycentric average would be strictly below the threshold. For a singleton the event implication is equality. Integrate this event inequality over each of the finite measures in (8) and over the singleton if present, then sum the orbits. Using the distinct source indices and (9) gives
\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}(H_{\mathbf J})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\nu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\mu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I}),
\]
including closed-boundary events and vertical halfspaces. This is (3).

Now take \(\rho=\delta_{\mathbf J}\otimes\kappa_{\mathbf J}\). It is a compactly supported log-concave measure on its affine support, since its relative density is the log-concave density in (10). The base projection is \(M\delta_{\mathbf J}\), so every projected closed halfspace containing \(\mathbf J\) has full mass \(M\). Apply accepted fact f049539ffd9c9b1d with \(z_0=\mathbf J\) and \(\alpha=1\). Its selection is \(\rho\) itself, and it gives \(\rho(H)\ge M/e\) for every closed ambient halfspace containing \((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star)\), the barycenter of \(\rho\). The centroid lies in \(\mathbf b+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\). Combining this bound with (3) proves the claimed actual mixed-integer depth at that one selected point.

We verify every original fiber in (4), independently of any unaccepted obstacle. Each condition \(z_i^2\le y_i\) is a convex epigraph condition. Together with \(y_i\le3\) it defines a closed, convex, bounded set, since \(|z_i|\le\sqrt3\) and \(0\le y_i\le3\). The point \(\mathbf z=\mathbf0\), \(\mathbf y=(3/2)\mathbf1_N\) satisfies every inequality strictly. Hence \(C_N\) is a convex body. Its entire nonempty lattice support is \(D_N=\{-1,0,1\}^N\), all these fibers have positive volume, and
\[
(C_N)_{\mathbf I}=\prod_{i=1}^N[I_i^2,3],
\qquad
w_{\mathbf I}=\prod_{i=1}^N(3-I_i^2),
\qquad
W=\prod_{i=1}^N(2+3+2)=7^N.
\tag{11}
\]
There are no further zero-volume nonempty lattice fibers. Every displayed fiber contains \(K=[1,3]^N\).

Use \(E=D_N\), \(\mathbf J=\mathbf0\), \(\mathbf b=\mathbf0\), \(A=0\), and \(\mathbf q=2\mathbf1_N\). Condition (1) holds for every original index. Here \(k_E=(3^N+1)/2\), \(\mathcal L^N(K)=2^N\), and the gauge is \(p_K(\mathbf x-\mathbf q)=\max_i|x_i-2|\). Thus the output cutoff in (6) is invariant under reflection in each coordinate about two. Its centroid is \(2\mathbf1_N\). Equation (7) gives the first inequality in (5). For the second,
\[
\frac{2^NM}{W}
\ge\frac14\left[\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)^N
                     +\left(\frac47\right)^N\right]
\ge\frac14\frac{12}{7}=\frac37,
\]
since \(N\ge1\) and \(12/7>1\).

To check the entropy claim, let \(U_K=2^{-N}\mathcal L^N|_K\), an auxiliary core law distinct from the original fiber laws. The original target law is \(U_{\mathbf0}=3^{-N}\mathcal L^N|_{[0,3]^N}\). The normalized output \(P=g\,d\mathbf x/G\) is supported in \(K\), has a bounded density, and obeys
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_{\mathbf0})
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_K)+N\log(3/2)
\ge N\log(3/2).
\]
The identity follows by taking the density ratio on \(K\); finiteness follows from boundedness and the convention \(0\log0=0\). The last inequality is Jensen's inequality for \(t\log t\) under \(U_K\). Thus the successful log-concave transport does not surreptitiously supply bounded relative entropy to the original uniform target law.

Finally verify the asserted consequence of the planar separating test, without claiming that its inequality has been proved. In the case \(n=d=1\), each positive fiber is a compact interval. Fix an allowed \(J,k\) in the definition of \(\mathcal B(C)\). If \(k>0\), let the midpoint of each of the two endpoint fibers be \(m_-\) and \(m_+\). Put
\(r=\min\{w_{J-k},w_{J+k}\}/2>0\),
\(b=(m_-+m_+)/2\), and \(a=(m_+-m_-)/(2k)\).
The two endpoint fibers contain, respectively, \(b-ak+[-r,r]\) and \(b+ak+[-r,r]\). Convexity of \(C\), using the same point of \([-r,r]\) in both endpoint intervals, implies
\(b+a(I-J)+[-r,r]\subseteq C_I\)
for every integer \(I\) between \(J-k\) and \(J+k\). Thus all these indices are in \(D\), and with this reflection-invariant set \(E\) and core \([-r,r]\), condition (1) holds. Here \(k_E=k+1\), so (2) gives mass at least
\((k+1)\min\{w_{J-k},w_{J+k}\}/2\).
If \(k=0\), use the midpoint and whole length of \(C_J\), with \(a=0\), to obtain the same bound. There are only finitely many allowed endpoint pairs, hence the maximum defining \(\mathcal B(C)\) is attained. Its proposed lower bound \(W/4\) would give mass at least \(W/8\). This last geometric inequality is the single unresolved test; none of the preceding theorem or box construction assumes it.
statement:
Retain \(C,S,h_S,C_{\mathbf I},\mu_{\mathbf I},w_{\mathbf I},D,U_{\mathbf I},W\) from accepted fact 793210f8a4be3647. In particular, \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body, \(n,d\ge1\), \(\mu_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}}\), \(w_{\mathbf I}=|\mu_{\mathbf I}|\), \(D=\{\mathbf I:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\), and \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}>0\).

Suppose that \(\mathbf J\in\mathbb Z^n\), that \(E\subseteq D\) is finite and nonempty with \(2\mathbf J-E=E\), that \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body, and that \(\mathbf b\in\mathbb R^d\) and a linear map \(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfy
\[
\mathbf b+A(\mathbf I-\mathbf J)+K\subseteq C_{\mathbf I}
\qquad(\mathbf I\in E).
\tag{1}
\]
Write \(k_E=(|E|+\mathbf1_{\{\mathbf J\in E\}})/2\), the number of orbits of \(E\) under reflection about \(\mathbf J\). There is a finite collection of barycentric source couplings, each with integral base barycenter \(\mathbf J\), such that their aggregate output measure \(\kappa_{\mathbf J}\) has a nonzero continuous log-concave density on \(\mathbb R^d\), is supported in \(C_{\mathbf J}\), and has mass
\[
M:=|\kappa_{\mathbf J}|\ge\frac{k_E}{2}\mathcal L^d(K).
\tag{2}
\]
At every original index, the sum of the actual source marginal measures of all these couplings is dominated by \(\mu_{\mathbf I}\). In fact each source in \(E\) is used in exactly one coupling, and no other source is used.

For every closed ambient halfspace \(H\), with section \(H_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in H\}\), these measures satisfy
\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}(H_{\mathbf J})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\mu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H).
\tag{3}
\]
Consequently the actual output centroid
\(\mathbf y^\star=M^{-1}\int\mathbf y\,d\kappa_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf y)\)
satisfies \((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star)\in S\) and
\(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star))\ge M/e\).
Here the centroid consumer is accepted fact f049539ffd9c9b1d, with a comparison supported on the already chosen integral fiber. It is not the original uniform-fiber centroid consumer.

In particular, for every integer \(N\ge1\), let \(n=d=N\) and
\[
C_N=\{(\mathbf z,\mathbf y)\in\mathbb R^N\times\mathbb R^N:
                z_i^2\le y_i\le3\ (1\le i\le N)\}.
\tag{4}
\]
At \(\mathbf J=\mathbf0\) the construction has a continuous log-concave output supported in \([1,3]^N\), with centroid \(2\mathbf1_N\), original source marginal domination, and
\[
M\ge2^{N-2}(3^N+1)
\ge\frac37\,2^{-N}W,
\qquad W=7^N.
\tag{5}
\]
For its normalized output \(P=\kappa_{\mathbf0}/M\), using exactly the normalization of \(P\) and \(U_{\mathbf J}\) in accepted fact 793210f8a4be3647, one nevertheless has
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_{\mathbf0})\ge N\log(3/2)\).
